The incident is caused by a scheduling deadlock on the recommendations-api deployment in namespace proofix-case-05. The deployment spec configures a strict podAntiAffinity rule (requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) with topologyKey kubernetes.io/hostname for pods matching label app.kubernetes.io/name=recommendations-api. With only one available worker node (vm-2) hosting a matching replica, the scheduler fails to place the remaining replica, resulting in FailedScheduling events and leaving the replica permanently Pending. The node has adequate CPU and memory without pressure conditions or taints blocking scheduling. The recovery is to change the pod anti-affinity rule from requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution to preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution with topologyKey kubernetes.io/hostname so replicas can be co-located when node capacity allows.

The recommendations-api deployment has 2 replicas configured with required hostname-level pod anti-affinity (podAntiAffinity.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution matching app.kubernetes.io/name=recommendations-api with topologyKey kubernetes.io/hostname). In the single-node cluster (vm-4), only one replica could be scheduled (recommendations-api-599d96d7cd-bh6xs) while the second replica (recommendations-api-599d96d7cd-6ztpf) remained in Pending state due to FailedScheduling (1 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules). Node resources (CPU/memory/PIDs) are sufficient and no taints or pressures block scheduling. To resolve the deadlock, the required anti-affinity rule must be relaxed to preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution or configured with a satisfiable topology domain.

The recommendations-api Deployment in namespace proofix-case-05 has a scheduling deadlock caused by a hard (required) podAntiAffinity rule with topologyKey 'kubernetes.io/hostname'. With only one eligible node (vm-4) in the cluster hosting an existing recommendations-api replica, the remaining replica cannot be scheduled and remains in Pending state with FailedScheduling events ('didn't match pod anti-affinity rules'). The node has sufficient allocatable resources and no pressure conditions or taints preventing scheduling. The root cause is the unsatisfiable required hostname anti-affinity rule on the single-node pool, which can be resolved by converting the rule to preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution or relaxing the topology domain.

The checkout-api deployment was unable to scale to its desired 3 replicas due to quota exhaustion on ResourceQuota 'case-06-cpu-budget' (hard limit: 500m requests.cpu, used: 500m). Namespace CPU requests were attributed to 2 running checkout-api pods (100m requests each, 200m total) and 1 stale-canary pod (300m requests). The stale-canary deployment was verified to be benchmark-owned (proofix.io/benchmark-owned: 'true') and carrying no live traffic (proofix.io/live-traffic: 'false', with no backend endpoints). Scaling down the stale-canary deployment to 0 replicas safely reclaims 300m of CPU quota, permitting checkout-api to schedule its third replica onto the available node capacity.

The incident CASE-06 (ResourceQuota saturation) in namespace proofix-case-06 is resolved. The ResourceQuota 'case-06-cpu-budget' was saturated at 500m requests.cpu (hard: 500m, used: 500m), preventing checkout-api from scaling to its desired 3 replicas (each requesting 100m CPU). The namespace CPU request quota was consumed by two running checkout-api pods (2x100m = 200m) and one benchmark-owned stale canary pod (300m CPU request) labeled with 'proofix.io/benchmark-owned: true' and 'proofix.io/live-traffic: false'. By scaling deployment/stale-canary to 0 replicas, 300m CPU request quota was reclaimed, allowing checkout-api's third replica to be admitted and scheduled on node vm-4 without modifying the ResourceQuota object or reducing safe container resource requests.

The pricing-api pod was repeatedly crashing with exit code 137 (OOMKilled) because the JVM maximum heap was configured to -Xmx512m within a container memory limit of 256Mi. Under load, PricingServer retained memory chunks scaled to maxMemory, exceeding the cgroup memory limit and causing OOM termination. Node vm-4 remained healthy without node memory pressure. The deployment was patched and successfully rolled out to resolve the heap and container memory limit mismatch.

The pricing-api pod was experiencing repeated CrashLoopBackOff and OOM terminations with exit code 137 and reason OOMKilled. The container was configured with a memory limit of 256Mi and request of 128Mi, while the JVM was configured with -Xmx512m (max heap ~512MB). PricingServer allocated memory chunks up to 70% of max heap (~360MB), causing the container to exceed its cgroup limit of 256Mi and trigger the kernel OOM killer. Node vm-4 remained healthy with no MemoryPressure and ample allocatable memory (16374180Ki), localizing the issue strictly to the container cgroup limit. The incident was resolved by patching the deployment resource/JVM configuration and successfully completing the rollout.

The root cause of incident CASE-08 is CPU throttling on the search-api container caused by an injected 100m CPU limit and request combined with a tight 1s liveness probe timeout. Under benchmark load, the /healthz endpoint (which executes 50ms of CPU work in SearchServer.java) competed for CPU cycles and exceeded the 1-second timeout, triggering kubelet Unhealthy probe failures and restart cascades (exit code 143). Node vm-4 has 4 allocatable CPUs and no resource pressure, confirming capacity. The remediation is to patch the search-api deployment to increase CPU request/limit (500m request / 1000m limit) and tune the liveness probe timeout to 3s with a failure threshold of 3.
HTTP 5xx rate exceeds 0.001, p95 latency exceeds 200ms, or search-api deployment rollout fails.

Root Cause Analysis:
1. Resource Starvation and CPU Throttling: The deployment `proofix-case-08/search-api` was injected with an aggressive CPU request and limit of 100m (`injected-100m-cpu`).
2. Liveness Probe Cascade: The Java application's `/healthz` endpoint executes CPU-intensive work (`burnCpuMicros(50_000)`). Under benchmark search traffic, the container experiences severe CFS CPU throttling against its 100m limit. As a result, the probe cannot complete within its configured 1-second timeout (`timeoutSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 2`), leading to repeated probe failures (`context deadline exceeded`).
3. Restart Loops & Degradation: After reaching the failure threshold, kubelet kills and restarts the container (observed exit code 143, restart count 3), precipitating an availability dip and latency spike.
4. Capacity Verification & Recovery: Node `vm-4` has 4 allocatable CPUs with no resource pressure. Remediation requires raising the search container's CPU request and limit to known-safe levels (e.g. 500m request / 1000m limit) and adjusting the liveness probe timeout (e.g. 3s timeout, failureThreshold 3) without disabling health monitoring.
Rollback if the deployment fails rollout, encounters CrashLoopBackOff, or fails to meet the SLO of p95 latency < 200ms and 5xx error rate < 0.001.

The incident was caused by a credential secret desynchronization between the database and the billing application. The database password was rotated to authoritative generation b9b26c30a42a65968efab3834749fdbf83374b60e371d95d1dc3ee3e8fd2a5ee (held in db-credentials), while the billing-api Deployment and running pod were consuming the stale credential generation 0aab604799348439ce4cc92447e78eebc30206aee3d5625982cddfd410238f40 from billing-credentials (resource version 113923). Network connectivity to PostgreSQL was healthy, but authentication was rejected by the database. The issue was resolved by synchronizing billing-credentials to the authoritative credential generation (digest b9b26c30a42a65968efab3834749fdbf83374b60e371d95d1dc3ee3e8fd2a5ee) and executing a controlled rollout of the billing-api Deployment.

The incident in CASE-11 was caused by the orders-consumer Deployment in namespace proofix-case-11 being scaled down from 3 replicas to 1 replica. With 6 topic partitions and an ingress rate of 42 records/second (with ~0.04s processing time per record), a single consumer replica was saturated at 25 records/second, causing continuous consumer lag growth. The deployment has been restored by scaling orders-consumer back to 3 replicas, enabling parallel partition consumption across the group to drain and bound consumer lag.
